outcome: As far as the sources show, the general statement is still open: no accepted proof exists. One single-author arXiv preprint (Glover, arXiv:2501.00614, first posted 31 Dec 2024, latest version v14 on 30 May 2026) claims a full proof; no referee report, journal acceptance or expert check of it was found. Partial results posted since 26 Jan 2024 are: a constant-factor improvement to 0.715538 (Huang and Peng, Dec 2024); random digraphs (Espuny Diaz et al., Mar 2024); tournaments missing two stars (Daamouch et al., Jun 2024); k-anti-transitive digraphs (Mezher and Daamouch, May 2024); a computer check for orders up to 7 (Halkiewicz, Jan 2026, later withdrawn in its latest version); a structural paper on near-counterexamples (Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld, Mar 2026); the minimum out-degree 7 case (Sadhukhan, Sandeep and Sen, Jun 2026); a stronger matching form (Bai, Li and Park, Jul 2026); and the order 2 delta + 2 case (Brukhman, Aug 2026).
problem_asks: The statement asks one thing. For every finite oriented graph D (a directed graph with no loops, no parallel arcs and no digons, i.e. no pair of opposite arcs): does there exist at least one vertex v such that the number of vertices at distance exactly two from v is at least the number at distance one? Read as out-distance, the standard reading, this is |N++(v)| >= |N+(v)|, where N+(v) is the set of out-neighbours of v and N++(v) is the set of vertices reached by a directed walk of length exactly two from v that are not out-neighbours of v (and not v itself). The statement does not say out- or in-distance; by reversing all arcs the two readings are the same problem. The statement asks for no bound, no constant, no count and no characterisation of the vertices. The tournament case (Dean's conjecture) is a special case, not a separate part. The question is 'every oriented graph has such a vertex' and nothing else.

events.what_happened: Espuny Diaz, Girao, Granet and Kronenberg, 'Seymour's second neighbourhood conjecture: random graphs and reductions' (arXiv:2403.02842). For each fixed p in [0,1/2), almost surely every orientation of the random graph G(n,p) satisfies the conjecture (and a related conjecture of Sullivan). They argue p = 1/2 is a natural barrier for the approach, and reduce a counterexample to one with large strongly connected examples of bounded minimum out-degree. The arXiv abstract page was read; the full text was not.
events.revisions: v1 5 Mar 2024; v2 9 Aug 2024. The arXiv comment says 'final version, to appear in Random Structures & Algorithms'.
events.delivers: Restricted to random digraphs: for fixed p below 1/2, almost every orientation of G(n,p) has a Seymour vertex. It says nothing about any fixed oriented graph. The reduction (any counterexample would be large, strongly connected, of bounded minimum out-degree) is conditional and is not a resolution.
events.remains: Every fixed oriented graph; the random model for p >= 1/2; the general statement.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed combinatorics journal; the authors are working combinatorialists
checked_by.what_they_did: Stated on arXiv as 'to appear'. I did not confirm that the paper was published.

events.direction: Partial and in the direction of the conjecture, for random digraphs only. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Mezher and Daamouch, 'A note on the second neighborhood problem for k-anti-transitive and m-free digraphs' (arXiv:2405.17797). Proves that if D is k-anti-transitive and (k-4)-free then D has a Seymour vertex. The paper notes this gives a special case of the Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture for 7-anti-transitive oriented graphs.
events.delivers: Restricted to the digraph classes k-anti-transitive and (k-4)-free, defined by forbidden structures. It does not cover oriented graphs in general.
events.remains: All oriented graphs outside those classes, which is nearly all of them.
events.time_since_posted: about 16 months; no journal reference shown on the arXiv page
events.direction: Partial and in the direction of the conjecture, for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Daamouch, Ghazal and Al-Mniny, 'About the second neighborhood conjecture for tournaments missing two stars or disjoint paths' (arXiv:2406.03635). The abstract's main sentence is 'In this paper, we prove SSNC for tournaments missing two stars.' The title also mentions disjoint paths; I did not confirm that result from the text I could read. The arXiv comment says 'Accepted in Contributions to Discrete Mathematics'.
events.delivers: Tournaments with two stars removed (a restricted class of near-tournaments). The disjoint-paths case is named in the title only, as far as I could confirm.
events.remains: Oriented graphs that are not tournaments missing two stars; the general statement. The disjoint-paths case, if it is a separate result, is unconfirmed.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted, according to the arXiv comment. Not confirmed on the journal's site.

events.direction: Partial and in the direction of the conjecture, for a restricted class of tournaments.

events.what_happened: Huang and Peng, 'An improved bound on Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture' (arXiv:2412.20234). Shows that every oriented graph has a vertex u with |N++(u)| >= 0.715538 |N+(u)|. This improves the Chen-Shen-Yuster constant 0.657298 (2003). The abstract describes it as the first improvement to the best constant in over two decades. The authors are at the National University of Singapore (per search snippet). A talk by Fei Peng at BIRS in June 2025 was found in search results; that is a talk, not a verification.
events.delivers: A constant-factor bound for the ratio |N++(u)|/|N+(u)| for some vertex u, in every oriented graph. The conjecture asserts that this ratio is at least 1 for some vertex, so this moves the best known ratio but does not reach the threshold 1. The ratio is a quantity the conjecture names, so the bound moves a quantity the problem asks about, while the problem remains open.
events.remains: The conjecture itself: a vertex with ratio at least 1.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture: a weaker constant-factor statement. Does not contradict the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Charles N. Glover, an independent researcher (Washington, DC), posted arXiv:2501.00614. The v1 title was 'An Algorithmic Approach to Finding Degree-Doubling Nodes in Oriented Graphs'. Its abstract says it 'presents a definitive proof of the conjecture by introducing the GLOVER (Graph Level Order) data structure'. The latest version, v14 (30 May 2026), is titled 'A Minimum Counterexample Proof of the Seymour Second Neighborhood Conjecture via the Graph Level Order', and its abstract calls it 'a constructive proof of the Seymour Second Neighborhood Conjecture (SSNC)'. The argument (as stated in the v14 abstract) classifies oriented graphs by minimum out-degree delta, builds a BFS-based rooted-neighbourhood structure from a minimum-out-degree root, and ends with a supply-demand argument: arc capacity is exhausted once the level index exceeds delta/3, so a Seymour vertex must exist in every graph. The v14 HTML was read: Section 5 gives a 'Main Theorem' (Theorem 5.1) about the last rooted neighbourhood, stated for a graph in which every vertex is non-Seymour, and Lemma 2.2 (Internal Degree Lower Bound) is the key lemma.
events.revisions: v1 31 Dec 2024; v2 6 Jan 2025; v3 8 Jan 2025; v4 9 Jan 2025; v5 13 Jan 2025; v6 21 Jan 2025; v7 28 Jan 2025; v8 4 Feb 2025; v9 19 Feb 2025 (438 KB); v10 23 Jun 2025 (885 KB); v11 2 Jul 2025 (661 KB); v12 9 Jul 2025 (668 KB); v13 21 Feb 2026 (64 KB); v14 30 May 2026 (29 KB, latest; no withdrawal note). The v1 abstract uses 'definitive'; the v14 abstract uses 'constructive'. The v14 comment reads '17 pages, 9 images. 4 tables. Cut out most of the fluff to trim the paper. Added section on further work'.
events.delivers: Claims the full statement: every oriented graph has a Seymour vertex. The claim covers all oriented graphs, with no restriction in its own statement. Nothing has been verified by anyone other than the author.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds. As far as the sources show, every part of the statement is claimed as settled and none has been independently confirmed.
events.time_since_posted: about 21 months since v1; latest version posted 30 May 2026 (about 4.5 months)
events.directly_checkable: No computation is claimed. The argument is a written proof of about 17 pages (v14 comment), so it can be checked by reading.
events.doubts: (1) Single-author preprint from an independent researcher with no journal venue. (2) Revised 13 times, with the abstract changing from 'definitive proof' (v1) to 'constructive proof' (v14) and the title from 'Algorithmic Approach' to 'Minimum Counterexample Proof'. The file size jumps from 43 KB (v1) to 885 KB (v10) and falls to 64 KB (v13). (3) A reader tool summarising the v14 HTML reported that Theorem 5.1 is stated under the hypothesis that every vertex is non-Seymour, which is the contradiction setting, and that the text omits several proofs ('many more proofs about the necessity of arcs would need to be adopted', Remark 2.1). I did not verify either point against the full text myself. (4) The Open Problem Garden page records earlier flawed claimed proofs of this same conjecture (2009; see the separate event). Those are different manuscripts, and I have not connected them to this one.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture for every oriented graph, which cuts in favour of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Stanislaw M. S. Halkiewicz, arXiv:2601.21563 (v1, 29 Jan 2026), 'Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture for Oriented Graphs of Order at Most Seven and Split-Twin Extensions'. By exhaustive computation the author checks that the second-neighbourhood invariant Delta(D) >= 0 for every oriented graph on at most seven vertices. The v1 HTML states the computation is a Julia 1.11.2 script (exhaustive_ratios.jl), run single-threaded on a laptop, with code at github.com/profsms/snc. The v1 also introduces a 'split-twin extension' operation. v2 (12 Mar 2026, retitled 'Split-Twin Extensions Preserving Seymour Vertices') proves that every split-twin extension at a vertex x not in N+(v) of a graph with a Seymour vertex v again has a Seymour vertex; with the Kaneko-Locke theorem this yields infinite classes of oriented graphs satisfying the conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2026 (13 KB); v2 12 Mar 2026 (8 KB; retitled); v3 21 May 2026 (not read); v4 23 Jul 2026 withdrawn by the author. See the separate event for the v4 listing.
events.delivers: Restricted: the statement for all oriented graphs on at most seven vertices (computer-verified, per the author), and infinite inductively generated families via the split-twin extension (v2 theorem plus Kaneko-Locke). It does not reach graphs of order eight or more outside those families.
events.remains: Oriented graphs of order 8 or more outside the split-twin families, which is the general statement.

machine_checked.system: Julia 1.11.2 exhaustive enumeration script (exhaustive_ratios.jl); not a proof assistant

events.directly_checkable: Enumeration of oriented graphs on at most seven vertices, with code linked from the v1 page. I did not run the code.
events.doubts: The small-order result rests on a computer enumeration that no one else has reported rerunning. The author withdrew the latest version (v4), without a stated reason on the listing (see the separate event).
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for small orders and for some infinite families. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: The arXiv listing for arXiv:2601.21563 at v4 (23 Jul 2026) is marked as withdrawn by the author. The abstract displayed on the abstract page for that listing is not the v1 abstract: it defines Pisa graphs as strongly connected oriented graphs with maximum vertex margin 0, proves that a Pisa graph with a vertex of out-degree one has underlying graph C_n, reports a computer check that every Pisa graph on at most seven vertices has underlying graph C_n or K_n minus a matching, and conjectures that every Pisa graph has underlying graph C_n or K_n minus a matching. It also mentions blow-up constructions of Zelenskyi, Darmosiuk and Nalivayko. The comments field reads: 'Counterexamples were found to the conjecture by four independent researchers, who contacted me about it'. The v3 text (21 May 2026) was not read, so I cannot say which version first carried the Pisa material.
events.revisions: v3 21 May 2026 (not read); v4 23 Jul 2026, withdrawn by the author. The date given is the v4 listing date; the Pisa content may date from v3 or earlier.
events.delivers: On the Pisa-graph class only: the out-degree-one case and a check on at most seven vertices. The abstract does not state a counterexample to Seymour's conjecture.
events.remains: The whole conjecture, and, on the Pisa class, the general Pisa conjecture.
events.time_since_posted: about 2.5 months since the v4 listing
events.doubts: The comment is ambiguous. Reading one: it refers to counterexamples to the paper's own Pisa-graph conjecture, which fits the abstract. Reading two: it refers to counterexamples to Seymour's conjecture itself. No counterexample object is described in any source I found. Other 2026 sources (Sadhukhan et al., June; Bai, Li and Park, July; Brukhman, August) still describe the conjecture as open, and Brukhman's abstract gives lower bounds on the order of any counterexample, not a counterexample. The v4 is withdrawn, so the claim cannot be checked on arXiv.

withdrawn.what: Version v4 of arXiv:2601.21563 is marked 'This paper has been withdrawn by Stanislaw Halkiewicz'. No reason is given on the listing.

events.direction: Ambiguous. On the Pisa class it is a structural statement. The comment, if read as about Seymour's conjecture, would cut against it, but no object is given.
events.object: No counterexample object is described in the abstract. The Pisa-graph structure is that a Pisa graph with a vertex of out-degree one has underlying graph C_n, and the conjecture is that every Pisa graph has underlying graph C_n or K_n minus a matching. The comment refers to counterexamples found by four unnamed researchers, which I could not locate.

events.what_happened: Krystal Guo, Ross J. Kang and Gabrielle Zwaneveld, 'Seymour-tight orientations' (arXiv:2603.29626, 31 Mar 2026). The paper studies near-counterexamples to the conjecture, which it calls Seymour-tight orientations. It shows the class is closed under generalized lexicographic products; that multiplying a putative counterexample by a Seymour-tight orientation yields another counterexample; and that if the conjecture is false, counterexamples close to regular tournaments exist. It also relates these to Sullivan's conjecture and to Cayley digraphs, using Kemperman's theorem for the abelian case. Abstract and HTML were read.
events.delivers: Conditional structure only: if the conjecture is false, there would be counterexamples of certain kinds. It does not establish any case of the conjecture.
events.remains: Everything. The paper does not decide the conjecture in any case.
events.direction: None established. The paper is conditional on the conjecture being false and does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Arpan Sadhukhan, R. B. Sandeep and Sagnik Sen, 'A proof of Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture for oriented graphs with minimum out-degree equal to 7' (arXiv:2606.30588, 29 Jun 2026). The abstract says the proof 'uses a sequence of local reductions, and the remaining finite cases are checked by computer', and that the work is 'partially computer-assisted: after a sequence of local reductions, the remaining finite obstruction models are eliminated by reproducible OR-Tools CP-SAT infeasibility checks.' The authors describe it as the first improvement of the minimum out-degree threshold in two decades, after Kaneko and Locke (2001) handled minimum out-degree at most 6. Section 2 says 'The CP-SAT models used in the computational part were developed with assistance from ChatGPT 5.5 Pro; the resulting OR-Tools CP-SAT encodings were then run and independently audited by the authors to verify that all corresponding finite configurations are infeasible.' Sections 3 and 4 say 'No computer search or certificate is used in this case.' Code is at github.com/rbsandeep/Seymour-Vertex-delta7.
events.revisions: v1 only (29 Jun 2026, 34 KB), as listed.
events.delivers: All oriented graphs of minimum out-degree exactly 7. Together with Kaneko-Locke (minimum out-degree at most 6), this covers every minimum out-degree up to 7, so any counterexample would need minimum out-degree at least 8.
events.remains: Oriented graphs of minimum out-degree at least 8, and therefore the general statement.

machine_checked.system: OR-Tools CP-SAT infeasibility checks (not a proof assistant). The encodings were written with ChatGPT 5.5 Pro assistance and run and audited by the authors.

events.directly_checkable: The local reductions in Sections 3 and 4 are written out and can be checked by hand; the finite configurations are checked by the linked CP-SAT encodings. I did not run the code.
events.doubts: Part of the proof rests on computer infeasibility checks. The encodings were written with ChatGPT 5.5 Pro's assistance and were audited by the authors themselves; I found no independent rerun. Single arXiv version, no peer review found.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for minimum out-degree 7. No counterexample.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.5 Pro
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors: assisted in developing the CP-SAT models used in the computational part of the proof (the finite infeasibility checks). The authors then ran and independently audited the resulting encodings themselves.
systems.basis_quote: The CP-SAT models used in the computational part were developed with assistance from ChatGPT 5.5 Pro;

events.what_happened: Yandong Bai, Binlong Li and Boram Park, 'Towards a strengthening of the second neighborhood conjecture' (arXiv:2607.18047, v1 20 Jul 2026, v2 24 Jul 2026). The paper studies a stronger property: a vertex x such that there is a complete matching from the out-neighbours of x into its second out-neighbours. Abstract: the stronger version holds for every oriented graph with minimum out-degree at most 5 and for every 5-anti-transitive oriented graph, and 'This implies that every oriented planar graph satisfies the stronger version.' Only the abstract was read.
events.delivers: A stronger form of the conjecture (complete matching from N+(x) into N++(x)) for minimum out-degree at most 5, for 5-anti-transitive graphs, and for planar graphs. The original conjecture is not settled. The minimum out-degree at most 5 case of the original is already covered by Kaneko-Locke (minimum out-degree at most 6), so the original gains nothing there.
events.remains: The original statement for general oriented graphs; the stronger matching form for general oriented graphs.
events.direction: Different question (a stronger form). Its results do not contradict the conjecture and do not settle it.

events.what_happened: Jake Brukhman (affiliation given as CoinFund), 'A dense-case theorem for Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture' (arXiv:2608.11530, 12 Aug 2026, 5 pages, math.CO). Theorem 1.1 (verbatim in the HTML): 'Let G be an oriented graph on n vertices with minimum outdegree delta. If n = 2delta+2, then G has a Seymour vertex.' Combined with Fisher's tournament theorem, this covers all oriented graphs with n at most 2delta+2 (per the abstract). The paper says the lower bound on the order of a counterexample rises from 16 to 17, or from 18 to 19 if the Sadhukhan et al. preprint is assumed. The acknowledgements, read from the HTML, credit AI systems (see the ai field). The author states: 'The author verified the proofs and accepts sole responsibility for the final manuscript and its claims.'
events.delivers: Restricted to oriented graphs of order exactly 2delta+2, where delta is the minimum out-degree, with no assumptions on the missing edges. The tournament case is already known (Fisher, 1996). Under the abstract's combination, all oriented graphs with n at most 2delta+2 are covered. Nothing is established for order 2delta+3 or larger relative to delta.
events.remains: Oriented graphs with n greater than 2delta+2, i.e. nearly all graphs of higher minimum out-degree, and the general statement.
events.directly_checkable: A 5-page counting argument for Theorem 1.1, readable by hand. I read only the HTML page; the full argument was not read by me.
events.doubts: Sole author. The acknowledgements say the key argument was found by an AI system: 'OpenAI language models (GPT-5 family) carried out the detailed mathematical exploration, implemented counterexample searches and verification tools, discovered the fixed-target capacity argument and its double-counting proof, and drafted the manuscript;'. The author states that he verified the proofs. I found no independent human check. The paper is short and self-contained, so an independent check is feasible.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for oriented graphs of order 2delta+2. No counterexample. It also gives a conditional bound on the order of any counterexample.

systems.name: OpenAI language models (GPT-5 family)
systems.what_it_did: Per the author's acknowledgements: carried out the detailed mathematical exploration, implemented counterexample searches and verification tools, discovered the fixed-target capacity argument and its double-counting proof, and drafted the manuscript. The author says he directed the investigation, selected the result, and verified the proofs.
systems.basis_quote: OpenAI language models (GPT-5 family) carried out the detailed mathematical exploration, implemented counterexample searches and verification tools, discovered the fixed-target capacity argument and its double-counting proof, and drafted the manuscript;

events.what_happened: Duke Math+ / Data+ 2025 project 'AI Powered Discovery of Counterexamples in Combinatorics' (led by Professor Fan Wei; project manager Raymond Sun; six undergraduate team members). The project page states: 'Through the development of an efficient AMCS search framework, we contributed new approaches and evidence relevant to the Second Neighborhood Conjecture', together with work on the Sidorenko conjecture and EFX allocations. No specific result, counterexample or bound for this conjecture is stated. The Duke poster PDF on bigdata.duke.edu (path dated 2025/01) returned 301 and then 404 at the redirected host, so it was not read.
events.delivers: Nothing stated beyond 'new approaches and evidence'. The project describes search methods only (reinforcement learning, gradient-based optimisation, AMCS).
events.remains: The whole conjecture.
events.doubts: The claim is a description of approaches and evidence, with no result stated, so there is nothing to check.

events.what_happened: Juan Liu, Hong Yang, Xindong Zhang and Hong-Jian Lai, 'Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture for Line Digraph of Digraph and Its Jump Digraph', Acta Mathematica Sinica, Chinese Series, 68(6): 937-952 (DOI 10.12386/A20240031). Journal dates: received 22 Feb 2024, accepted 17 Jun 2024, published online 15 Nov 2025, issue 30 Dec 2025. No arXiv or other public preprint was found. The publisher's abstract did not load (it shows an unfilled template placeholder), so the result itself is not established.

events.delivers: Not established. The title indicates the conjecture is studied for line digraphs and their jump digraphs; I did not read the result.
events.remains: Not established.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (journal's accepted date 17 Jun 2024)

events.what_happened: Jiangdong Ai, Stefanie Gerke, Gregory Gutin, Shujing Wang, Anders Yeo and Yacong Zhou, 'On Seymour's and Sullivan's second neighbourhood conjectures' (arXiv:2306.03493). Version 1 (6 Jun 2023) is before the window. I could not read the full v1 text, so its results on Seymour's conjecture are not established. Version 2 (15 Jul 2026) acknowledges: 'This version of the paper corrects a mistake in the proof of Corollary 10' ... 'which was pointed to us by Emanuele Natale and Edouard Oyallon on July 10, 2026.' Corollary 10 states: 'Every planar oriented graph D=(V,A) has a Sullivan vertex.' That is Sullivan's conjecture, not Seymour's.
events.revisions: v1 6 Jun 2023; v2 15 Jul 2026, which corrects the proof of Corollary 10 (a planar Sullivan-vertex result). The arXiv comment on the abstract page reads '15 pages, 1 figures'. No journal reference is shown on the abstract page; a search snippet suggests the Journal of Graph Theory published it in 2024, which I did not confirm.
events.delivers: Not established for Seymour's conjecture: the v1 results could not be read. Corollary 10 concerns Sullivan's conjecture. A separate planar remark about Seymour's conjecture is mentioned in a summary of the HTML, not verified.
events.remains: Seymour's conjecture in general, unless the v1 results cover more than I could confirm.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years for v1; v2 posted 15 Jul 2026

events.what_happened: David C. Fisher, 'Squaring a tournament: a proof of Dean's conjecture', Journal of Graph Theory 23 (1996) 43-48. Proves that the conjecture holds for tournaments (Dean's conjecture). The Wikipedia article gives 1996. Not opened directly; the 1996 date and the tournament statement come from the Wikipedia article, and the Farkas-lemma method comes from a search snippet.
events.delivers: The conjecture for every tournament. Restricted to tournaments.
events.remains: Every oriented graph that is not a tournament.

checked_by.who: Journal of Graph Theory (journal of record)

events.what_happened: Frederic Havet and Stephan Thomasse gave a second, different proof of the tournament case using median orders (2000, per search snippets and secondary sources; not opened). A sinkless tournament has at least two Seymour vertices (per the same snippets).
events.delivers: Tournaments only (second proof), plus the stronger two-vertex statement for sinkless tournaments.
events.remains: Every oriented graph that is not a tournament.

events.what_happened: Yoshihiro Kaneko and Stephen C. Locke proved the conjecture for oriented graphs with minimum out-degree at most 6. The date 2001 comes from the Wikipedia article and from the Sadhukhan et al. preprint, which both give 2001. The venue was not confirmed.
events.delivers: Oriented graphs with minimum out-degree at most 6. The Wikipedia article says this implies the statement for graphs with at most 14 vertices, extended to 15.
events.remains: Oriented graphs with minimum out-degree 7 or more (until Sadhukhan et al., Jun 2026).
events.direction: Positive, in the direction of the conjecture, for minimum out-degree at most 6.

events.what_happened: Guantao Chen, Jian Shen and Raphael Yuster, 'Second neighborhood via first neighborhood in digraphs', Annals of Combinatorics 7 (2003) 15-20. Shows that every simple digraph without loops or digons has a vertex v with |N++(v)| >= gamma |N+(v)|, where gamma = 0.657298... is the real root of 2x^3 + x^2 - 1 = 0. The 2003 date comes from the Wikipedia article; the constant comes from the Open Problem Garden page and search snippets. The paper itself was not read.
events.delivers: A constant-factor version of the conjecture for every simple digraph (gamma approximately 0.657). The threshold 1 is not reached.
events.remains: The threshold 1 for the ratio, i.e. the conjecture itself.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture (a weaker ratio).

events.what_happened: Bin Chen and An Chang, 'Seymour's second neighborhood in 3-free digraphs', Annals of Applied Mathematics 35(4) (issue labelled 2019; pages say published online Aug 2020, per a search snippet). Shows that every 3-free digraph has a vertex v with d++(v) >= floor(lambda d+(v)), lambda = 0.6958. Not opened; the details come from search snippets.
events.revisions: Dates differ between the issue label (2019) and the online date (Aug 2020), both before the window.
events.delivers: A constant-factor version for 3-free digraphs. Restricted class.
events.remains: The threshold 1 for 3-free digraphs and the general statement.

checked_by.who: Annals of Applied Mathematics (journal of record)

events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Fidler and Yuster (2007): the conjecture holds for dense incomplete cases where the missing edges form a matching, a star, or a clique (as cited by Brukhman, 2026). Not opened; date from the citation in Brukhman's preprint.
events.delivers: Dense incomplete digraphs whose missing edges form a matching, a star, or a clique (per the citation).
events.remains: The general statement.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for restricted dense classes.

events.what_happened: James Brantner, Greg Brockman, Bill Kay and Emma E. Snively, 'Contributions to Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture' (arXiv:0808.0946, submitted 7 Aug 2008; 9 pages, 4 figures). Gives sufficient conditions and classes of digraphs for which the conjecture holds, and shows that a counterexample, if one exists, would have to have certain properties. The Wikipedia article (dated 2009, presumably the journal year) says the authors showed that in triangle-free orientations a vertex of minimum out-degree is a Seymour vertex. Only the first two sentences of the abstract were read.
events.delivers: Restricted: triangle-free orientations, and other classes the paper identifies. No resolution of the general statement.
events.remains: The general statement and the other classes not covered.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for restricted classes.

events.what_happened: Zachary Cohn and coauthors showed that random tournaments and some random digraphs have many Seymour vertices with high probability (2016, per the Wikipedia article; not opened directly).
events.delivers: A probabilistic statement about random tournaments and random digraphs. Not a case of the statement for every oriented graph.
events.remains: The general statement.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for random models.

events.what_happened: Tyler Seacrest, 'The arc-weighted version of the second neighborhood conjecture' (arXiv:1212.1883, Dec 2012; 10 pages, 3 figures). The abstract's first two sentences were read: the conjecture is 'verified in several special cases, most notably for tournaments by Fisher'. The arc-weighted statement is from the title; a search snippet says it strengthens Fisher's theorem.
events.delivers: An arc-weighted variant, which strengthens the tournament case per a search snippet. Not the unweighted conjecture for general oriented graphs.
events.remains: The unweighted conjecture for general oriented graphs.
events.direction: A variant, not the statement. Positive for tournaments in the variant.

events.what_happened: Salman Ghazal, 'The second neighborhood conjecture for oriented graphs missing combs' (arXiv:1602.08631, 27 Feb 2016). Shows the conjecture holds for oriented graphs missing a comb (the abstract was read only to its opening clause). Search snippets say the same argument covers oriented comb and threshold graphs.
events.delivers: Restricted: oriented graphs whose underlying missing structure is a comb (and, per snippet, threshold graphs).
events.remains: The general statement and other missing structures.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Tyler Seacrest, 'Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture for subsets of vertices' (arXiv:1808.06293, 20 Aug 2018). Proves that the conjecture is equivalent to: every oriented simple graph contains a subset S of vertices whose second neighbourhood is at least as large as its first.
events.delivers: A reformulation: an equivalent statement over subsets. No case is settled.
events.remains: The whole statement, equivalently.

events.what_happened: Suresh Dara and coauthors (2022, per the Wikipedia article): the conjecture holds for all oriented bipartite graphs, and for graphs whose vertices split into an independent set and a 2-degenerate graph. Not opened directly; the statement comes from the Wikipedia article.
events.delivers: Oriented bipartite graphs, and graphs whose vertices split into an independent set and a 2-degenerate graph.
events.remains: The general statement.
events.direction: Partial, in the direction of the conjecture, for restricted classes.

events.what_happened: Zelenskiy, Darmosiuk and Nalivayko, 'Properties of possible counterexamples to the Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture', Opuscula Mathematica 41(4) (2021) 601-605 (per search snippets; not opened). Argues that any counterexample would be strongly connected and could exist at both low and high density, and can be built with any diameter k >= 3.
events.delivers: Structural constraints on any counterexample. Does not settle the conjecture.
events.remains: The whole statement.

events.what_happened: Open Problem Garden entry for the conjecture (opened). An anonymous comment on 12 Dec 2009 says 'This conjecture has been proved' and links to a proof manuscript (the manuscript was not reachable from the page text). The same day, Robert Samal replied 'The proof, however, seems flawed', identifying Lemma 2 of the manuscript as not true and giving a counterexample (a directed cycle with many independent vertices joined from the cycle, where no cycle vertex satisfies the conjecture). A March 2010 and an August 2010 comment ask whether the proof is valid and say it is not. A 2011 comment (sjcjoosten) says 'Lemma 2 is false' and notes that its counterexample has two sinks, so it does not counter the conjecture itself.
events.revisions: Comments: 12 Dec 2009 (claim and critique), 14 Mar 2010, 8 Aug 2010, 18 Mar 2011. The manuscript's own date is not known.
events.delivers: A claimed full proof. Per the commenters, its Lemma 2 is false, so the claim does not hold as written.
events.remains: The whole statement, unless the manuscript has a repair, which no comment reports.

checked_by.who: Robert Samal (named commenter; qualifications not checked)
checked_by.qualification: Named commenter on the Open Problem Garden page
checked_by.what_they_did: Identified Lemma 2 as false and gave a counterexample to the lemma's use

events.doubts: Lemma 2 is reported false by two commenters. The 2011 commenter's counterexample is to the lemma, not to the conjecture.
events.direction: A claimed proof that cuts in favour of the conjecture, disputed on its key lemma.

events.what_happened: Tim Verheijen's problem page at Radboud University (opened, last updated 2007) says that a student, Brett Harrison, received 25,000 dollars from the Davidson Institute for Talent Development in 2005 for a proof that is 'supposedly more precise than the conjecture'. The page says that proof could not be found online and that the author had not contacted Harrison. The same page quotes Paul Seymour as saying that earlier proofs were wrong, and that 'an errorless proof of SSNC has not been found yet'.
events.delivers: Not established. The claimed proof is described as of a more precise statement than the conjecture, so it may be a different question.
events.remains: Not established.
events.doubts: The proof could not be located by the page's author, and the page says the author had not contacted the claimant.

events.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture' (OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims Theorem 1.1: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex v with |N₁⁺(v)| ≤ |N₂⁺(v)|, where N₂⁺(v) is the set of vertices at exact directed distance two from v (excluding v and its out-neighbours, each counted once). The proof is by contradiction. Proposition 2.1 reduces a minimal counterexample (fewest vertices, then fewest arcs) to a graph G with positive indegrees in which every nonempty proper vertex set U satisfies |U| + |F²(U)| < 2|F(U)|, where F is the one-step out-image; Lemma 2.2 (subset deficit, adapted from Seacrest's Lemma 4) and Lemma 2.3 (transitive-tournament blow-up) give this. Section 3 (Lemma 3.1, a pruning bound for two families of ordered pairs, proved by a rank/matching argument) and Proposition 4.1 then rule out any such G. The same manuscript also derives, in Section 5 (Corollary 5.1) via Seacrest's 2015 equivalences, vertex-weighted forms (for every nonnegative vertex weighting some v has η(N₁⁺(v)) ≤ η(N₂⁺(v)); and a total-mass-one weighting under which every v satisfies this) and an arc-weighted form, and in Section 6 (Corollary 6.1) directed-cycle consequences: a digraph with no directed triangle has some v with d⁺(v) ≤ |Z(v)| and n−1 ≥ 2d⁺(v)+d⁻(v); minimum in- and outdegree at least n/3 forces a directed triangle; and a regular digraph with d⁺ = d⁻ = r and directed girth 4 has n ≥ 3r+1.
events.delivers: Claims to settle the problem as the list states it. The list asks whether every oriented graph (no loops, no parallel arcs, no digons) has a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance two as at distance one. Theorem 1.1 gives exactly that, for every nonempty finite oriented graph, with no connectivity, degree or order hypothesis; a sink satisfies it trivially. The manuscript measures out-distance; reversing all arcs gives the in-distance reading, so both readings are covered. Tournaments, the special case known as Dean's conjecture, are covered by the general statement. The manuscript's wording matches the list's: its abstract says it 'resolves Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture positively', and Section 1 calls Theorem 1.1 that resolution.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim is correct: the problem asks only for the existence of such a vertex in every oriented graph, which Theorem 1.1 states. The weighted forms and directed-cycle consequences (Sections 5 and 6) go beyond what the problem asks.

machine_checked.scope: Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture asserts that every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many second out-neighbors as first out-neighbors. The formalized result proves this assertion, where the second neighborhood consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two. The initial vertex and first neighbors are excluded from that count, and sinks are included.

events.doubts: The argument is a long contradiction proof across Sections 2 to 4. Its most compressed step is the choice of coefficients in Lemma 3.1: the text relies on the cited Edmonds correspondence and a brief argument that the required minors can be nonzero at one real assignment (a product of nonzero polynomials). It does not flag this as sketched, but it is the least expanded part. The manuscript reports no computer verification. Its weighted and arc-weighted consequences depend on Seacrest's equivalences, which it cites and does not reprove.; conditional on: None for Theorem 1.1 beyond published results it cites: Edmonds (1967) for the generic-rank/matching correspondence used in Lemma 3.1, and König's theorem (re-derived in the text). Corollary 5.1 (weighted and arc-weighted forms) rests on Seacrest (2015), Proposition 2 and Theorem 1, cited rather than proved in the manuscript; that dependence does not affect the problem's own statement.

disputes.summary: Glover's arXiv preprint (v1 Dec 2024, v14 May 2026) claims the full statement. The other 2026 papers in the record (Sadhukhan et al., June; Bai, Li and Park, July; Brukhman, August) treat the conjecture as open and cite no acceptance of Glover's argument. No expert endorsement or refutation of Glover was found, so this is a status conflict with no expert resolution.

Halkiewicz's withdrawn v4 comment says counterexamples 'were found to the conjecture by four independent researchers'. Its abstract reads as about Pisa graphs, so the comment may concern the paper's own Pisa conjecture. No counterexample to Seymour's conjecture is named in any source, and the 2026 papers that bound counterexample orders (Brukhman: 17, or 19 conditional on Sadhukhan et al.) treat the conjecture as open.

The 2009 anonymous claimed proof (Open Problem Garden) was disputed by Samal in the same thread, and the dispute is about its Lemma 2. Its manuscript was not reachable from the page. Recorded for completeness; it is not the same manuscript as Glover's.

summary: The problem is open as far as the sources show. I ran 34 searches and opened 40 or more pages, including the arXiv abstract and HTML pages of every 2024-2026 preprint I found, the Wikipedia article, the Open Problem Garden entry, two Radboud problem pages, the Duke Math+ project page, the Acta Mathematica Sinica page for Liu et al., and the GitHub repository of Sadhukhan et al. Many arXiv PDFs returned compressed binary and I used HTML instead; the Brukhman, Sadhukhan and Ai et al. PDFs were not readable as text, and several quotes come from a fetch tool that summarises pages, so each quote should be rechecked against the source. The in-window events are: Espuny Diaz et al. (random digraphs, Mar 2024); Mezher and Daamouch (k-anti-transitive digraphs, May 2024); Daamouch et al. (tournaments missing two stars, Jun 2024); Huang and Peng (constant 0.715538, Dec 2024); Glover (claimed full proof, Dec 2024, v14 May 2026); Halkiewicz (orders up to 7 and split-twin extensions, Jan 2026; latest version withdrawn Jul 2026); Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld (conditional structure, Mar 2026); Sadhukhan, Sandeep and Sen (minimum out-degree 7, Jun 2026); Bai, Li and Park (stronger matching form, Jul 2026); Brukhman (order 2delta+2, Aug 2026); a Duke project claiming approaches and evidence (2025, no result); Liu et al. (line digraphs, journal 2025, public date unknown); and a 2026 revision of Ai et al. (a correction to a Sullivan-vertex corollary, not this conjecture). The Glover claim is the only one that, if correct, settles the whole statement. Nothing in the record has been refereed beyond journal acceptance of the older results, and no expert has publicly verified or refuted Glover. The AI picture is two load-bearing or computational credits: Brukhman credits OpenAI GPT-5-family models with discovering the key fixed-target capacity argument and its double-counting proof, and the author states he verified the proofs; Sadhukhan et al. credit ChatGPT 5.5 Pro with developing the CP-SAT encodings for the finite cases, which the authors then ran and audited themselves. Two further AI credits are recorded but excluded from the systems list because they concern checking or revision only: 'ChatGPT 5.5 Plus and Pro models for mathematical checks for any possible errors in parts of the paper' (Sadhukhan et al.), and 'Anthropic Claude models performed an adversarial audit of an intermediate draft and assisted with revisions' (Brukhman). Glover's full text, read through the v14 HTML, names no AI system. Close calls: (a) whether Sadhukhan et al.'s computer-assisted minimum-out-degree-7 case is a restricted class or a partial step (I treat it as a restricted class); (b) whether Huang and Peng's constant moves a quantity the conjecture names (I say yes, but it does not reach the threshold 1); (c) whether the ChatGPT-assisted CP-SAT encodings count as load-bearing AI work (I included them in systems because they are the computational proof of the finite cases, but the authors describe the assistance as developing models, not as the mathematics); (d) whether the Halkiewicz comment means counterexamples to Seymour's conjecture or to the paper's Pisa conjecture (the abstract favours the second, but the wording is open). Pre-window history is recorded as events: Fisher (1996, tournaments), Havet and Thomasse (2000), Kaneko and Locke (2001, minimum out-degree at most 6), Chen, Shen and Yuster (2003, constant 0.657), Fidler and Yuster (2007), Brantner et al. (2008), Seacrest (2012, 2018), Ghazal (2016), Cohn et al. (2016), Dara et al. (2022), Zelenskiy et al. (2021), the 2009 claimed proof and its dispute, and the 2005 claimed proof on the Radboud page. The posing paper of Dean and Latka (1995) is background, not a result, and is in the summary only.
competing_reading: The strongest reading for a settled problem: Glover's arXiv proof (v1 Dec 2024, v14 May 2026) is correct, and the statement has been solved since its latest version. The Glover text, as summarised, has a proof by contradiction over a minimum counterexample, and a short independent check of its key lemma could confirm or refute that. The later 2026 papers do not engage with it, which is consistent with either reading. Against settlement: no referee or expert has engaged with the text publicly, its revisions changed both the abstract and the title, and the summaries I read report omitted proofs. The reading I think the evidence supports is 'open, with an unverified full claim', but that rests on the absence of engagement, not on a checked error.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or a published expert verification or refutation of Glover's arXiv:2501.00614 (any version), with the specific lemma named. (2) An independent check of Brukhman's counting argument for n = 2delta+2 (5 pages) and of Sadhukhan et al.'s reductions and CP-SAT encodings. (3) The v3 text and the surrounding comment of Halkiewicz's arXiv:2601.21563, to tell whether the 'four independent researchers' comment refers to counterexamples to Seymour's conjecture. (4) The full text of Liu et al. (line digraphs) and of Ai et al. v1 (which contains Seymour results I could not read), to establish whether either bears on the statement. (5) The full text of Huang and Peng and of Espuny Diaz et al., to confirm the scope of their statements.

events.credibility_reason: Several F10 signals together: a landmark claim with no expert uptake in ~21 months; independent author outside the field; 14 revisions with title and framing changing and file size swinging 43KB->885KB->29KB; later 2026 papers by working combinatorialists still call the conjecture open and do not cite it; reported omitted proofs (Remark 2.1).
The author withdrew the arXiv paper (v4, 23 Jul 2026). The order-at-most-7 check is in any case only instances already implied by Kaneko-Locke; the split-twin families are the case content.
Withdrawn by the author, with a comment saying counterexamples were found; the content concerns the paper's own Pisa-graph conjecture, and no counterexample to Seymour's conjecture is described.

judgement.why: The OpenAI manuscript's Theorem 1.1 is stated for every nonempty finite oriented graph, which matches the statement word for word, so its scope is whole. It is only 8 days old, and the only check is a Lean build whose sorry-free status is not recorded (F7), so it is unreviewed. That is not a reason for doubt (F10), so it is credible. The README says the results came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model, so it is generated. Glover's claim is also whole in scope, but it has several F10 signals at once: an independent author, 14 revisions with the title and framing changing, no uptake in about 21 months, and later papers by specialists that still call the problem open. So it is not_credible. Brukhman's AI credit says the model discovered the key argument and its proof, which makes it generated. Sadhukhan et al.'s credit says ChatGPT helped develop the CP-SAT encodings, which are verification code that the authors then ran and audited themselves. Under F12 that is none, but it is a close call. Halkiewicz's paper was withdrawn by its author, so both of its rows are knocked_down. Espuny Diaz et al. is an 'almost every graph' statement about a random model rather than a class of graphs, so I scored it as bound (a proportion) and not as case. Bai, Li and Park prove a stronger matching form, and its only new territory for the original question is planar and 5-anti-transitive graphs, so I scored it as a variant. The Liu et al. date cannot be placed.
judgement.doubts: There are two close calls. (1) Sadhukhan et al.: the AI-developed CP-SAT encodings carry the finite cases of the proof, so 'assisted' is a defensible alternative to 'none'. The quote only says 'with assistance', and I judged that too thin. (2) The OpenAI attribution rests on a README sentence covering the 'vast majority' of results, not one specific to this manuscript. The Lean scope text matches the statement, but sorry_free is null. The result has not been independently verified, and its correctness is untested after 8 days. Liu et al.'s actual result was never read, so its scope as a case rests on the title alone.
